reading.body:
Carlyle Thorsen's AI lobbying is concentrated in copyright and creative-industry clients, not in the compute or data-center side of AI policy.

The client list is the story. Theatrical stage employees, the Directors Guild, the Copyright Clearance Center, the International Trademark Association, and the music publishers' advocacy arm all appear, alongside Bria Artificial Intelligence and Comcast. That is a coalition organized around training data, authorship, and rights clearance. The bills named, seven of them from 2025 or later, are the legislative surface of that fight.

The filings also disclose prior government service: General Counsel to Representative Tom DeLay, Deputy Assistant Attorney General, counsel on the House Judiciary Committee. Judiciary is where copyright and AI bills are referred, so the disclosed history is directly relevant to the subject matter, though the data records the positions and draws no conclusion from them.

What this does not cover is scale or outcome. Fifty-nine filings and seventeen entries say nothing about spending, whether any bill moved, or what the clients won. It also says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, and it should not be read as evidence about them. The grid is not part of this record.
